newsitem.title: UK: Experts call for better chronic fatigue treatment.
newsitem.headline: Experts call for better chronic fatigue treatment.

text.p: British experts on Wednesday laid to rest doubts that chronic fatigue was a real illness, saying it was an important condition that must be treated medically and psychologically.

Chronic Fatigue Sydrome, an ailment characterised by six months of severe fatigue that is made worse by physical or mental exertion, afflicts up to two percent of the population and has no evident underlying cause.
"CFS exists. It is a problem and it is not uncommon," doctor Simon Wessely told a news conference to launch probably the most thorough report on the illness.

Wessely, one of 16 doctors who contributed to the joint report of the Royal Colleges of Physicians, Psychiatrists and General Practitioners, said CFS -- often called yuppy flu -- was not linked to any social class or occupation.

Confusion surrounding the ailment led to suggestions that patients were imagining their health problems because its causes were unknown and its symptoms -- tiredness, muscle pain and depression -- are both physical and psychological.
"It is in that grey area (of medicine) that CFS sits," he said. Wessely and his colleagues disassociated CFS from myalgic encephalomyelitis (ME), a label used to cover a wide range of illness.
The cause of CFS, sometimes attributed to a virus, has not been identified, It causes debilitating symptoms which can last for years and some sufferers are too exhausted to work or lead normal lives.
The report called for a joint medical and psychological approach for treatment. Existing treatments such as complementary therapy, dietary changes and bed rest have not been effective.

Instead the report suggested graded exercise programmes, controlled clinical trials of anti-depressants for some sufferers and cognitive behaviour therapy, which is designed to help people cope with stress and emotional problems.
"It is done in collaboration with patients to help them understand their illness," Wessely explained.
The report also called for more research into all aspects of the illness and into its long-term consequences.

"It's time to abandon sterile arguments over whether CFS and ME are physical or mental illnesses and move on and promote more research into the management of this debilitating condition," said Robert Kendell, president of the Royal College of Psychiatrists.
